You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

You are the NOTION OWNER for a research-group documentation task. Your job: create structured Notion pages for exactly three analyzed papers, using ONLY the Notion MCP tools (mcp__notion__API-*). You must NOT create, modify, or send any email, and you must NOT touch any Word document or any filesystem files. Use only the canonical packet below — do not re-research the papers, do not add outside knowledge.

WORKSPACE CONTEXT: This is a research group's Notion workspace. The three papers were analyzed by the coordinator; you materialize the notes as Notion pages.

CANONICAL THREE-PAPER PACKET (verbatim facts to use):

PAPER 1:
- arXiv ID: 2301.07041
- Title: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"
- Authors (as returned by database): Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan
- Section structure: Introduction; Scaling Laws; Experiments; Conclusion
- Main contributions: Establishes empirical scaling laws for language model performance measured by cross-entropy loss; loss follows a power law with model size (N), dataset size (D), and compute (C); provides a principled framework for predicting model performance and allocating a fixed compute budget optimally; shows architectural details such as width/depth have minimal effects within a wide range.
- Methodology: Trained over 1000 models spanning roughly three orders of magnitude in scale; systematically varied model size, dataset size, and compute; measured cross-entropy loss and fitted power-law relationships L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N, with analogous relations for dataset size and compute; studied dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size and of training speed on model size.
- Key findings: Loss scales as a power law with exponents approximately alpha_N = 0.076, alpha_D = 0.095, alpha_C = 0.050, with trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude; larger models trained on more data with more compute consistently achieve lower loss; larger models are more sample-efficient; simple equations govern overfitting and training-speed dependencies.

PAPER 2:
- arXiv ID: 2203.11171
- Title: "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"
- Authors (as returned by database): Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang
- Section structure: Introduction; Method; Experiments; Results
- Main contributions: Introduces InstructGPT, language models fine-tuned to better follow user instructions; demonstrates that RLHF produces models strongly preferred by human labelers over much larger baselines; shows alignment improvements (truthfulness, toxicity) while keeping the model small (1.3B vs 175B GPT-3).
- Methodology: Three-step pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human-written demonstration data; (2) training a reward model from human preference comparisons; (3) further fine-tuning with reinforcement learning (PPO) using the reward model — collectively Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), starting from GPT-3.
- Key findings: InstructGPT 1.3B outputs are preferred by human evaluators over GPT-3 175B outputs on 85% of prompts; InstructGPT is more truthful (better on TruthfulQA) and less toxic; RLHF yields substantial alignment improvement with minimal trade-off in general capabilities.

PAPER 3:
- arXiv ID: 2205.01068
- Title: "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models"
- Authors (as returned by database): Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal
- Section structure: Introduction; Architecture; Training; Results
- Main contributions: Presents OPT, a suite of fully open-source large language models ranging from 125M to 175B parameters; models match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks; releases model weights and training code so the research community can study large language models.
- Methodology: Standard transformer architecture with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings; trained with the AdamW optimizer; trained on a corpus of roughly 800GB combining Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets; used tensor and pipeline parallelism across up to 992 A100 GPUs.
- Key findings: OPT-175B matches GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks; full public release of weights and training code enables community study of LLMs; documents training methodology, hardware infrastructure, and lessons learned from training at scale.

PROCEDURE (idempotent, exactly once per paper):
For EACH of the three papers, in this order (PAPER 1, PAPER 2, PAPER 3):
1. SEARCH for an existing page with exact title "Paper: <canonical title>" using mcp__notion__API-post-search with query "Paper: <canonical title>" and filter {"property":"object","value":"page"} (also check page_size 100). Examine results:
   - If EXACTLY ONE page has title exactly "Paper: <canonical title>": REUSE it. Do not create a new page. Optionally verify/leave its content as-is; record its page id.
   - If TWO OR MORE pages match exactly: BLOCK — do NOT create; record the duplicate IDs and flag this in your report.
   - If ZERO matches: CREATE exactly one page via mcp__notion__API-post-page with properties {"title": {"title": [{"text": {"content": "Paper: <canonical title>"}}]}} and the parent set to {"type":"workspace","workspace":true} if the API accepts it; if workspace-root creation fails, create it under the most recently edited existing page you find via search, and record which parent you used.
2. POPULATE the page body with structured notes. If you created a new page, pass the children in the create call; if you reused an existing page, append blocks via mcp__notion__API-patch-block-children. Body structure per page:
   - heading_2 "Overview" + paragraph(s): arXiv ID, authors, section structure (e.g., "Sections: Introduction; Scaling Laws; Experiments; Conclusion").
   - heading_2 "Main Contributions" + bulleted_list_item blocks (one bullet per contribution bullet from the packet).
   - heading_2 "Methodology" + bulleted_list_item blocks (one bullet per methodology bullet).
   - heading_2 "Key Findings" + bulleted_list_item blocks (one bullet per finding bullet).
   Use block type "heading_2" and "bulleted_list_item" with {"rich_text":[{"text":{"content":"..."}}]} payloads.

VERIFICATION (mandatory):
3. READ BACK every page you own: call mcp__notion__API-retrieve-a-page for each page id to confirm the title, and mcp__notion__API-get-block-children to confirm the body blocks exist (Overview / Main Contributions / Methodology / Key Findings headings present, and at least one bullet under each).
4. RETURN a structured report containing: for each paper — the final page id, the exact page title (must equal "Paper: <canonical title>"), arXiv ID coverage, whether created/reused/blocked, parent used, and block-validation result (headings present: yes/no). Also list any duplicate/blocked situations explicitly.

Acceptance criteria: exactly three pages (or fewer if exact matches were reused), each titled exactly "Paper: <title>", each with the four required content blocks containing the packet's facts. No emails sent, no Word/filesystem work done.

Your job: produce exactly one Word document at the path below, using ONLY the canonical packet provided — do not re-research the papers, do not add outside knowledge. You must NOT create or modify Notion pages, and you must NOT send any email.

WORKSPACE ROOT (frozen): /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-latex-analysis-notion-word/workspace
TARGET FILE: <workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx  (i.e. /workspace/dumps/kimi-code_DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-latex-analysis-notion-word/workspace/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx)

Build the document with python-docx (run via mcp__local__python_execute). It is strongly preferred that the file be created/written atomically: build the document in memory and write it once (e.g., write to a temp file then os.replace() to the final path, or simply a single save) so the file exists exactly once with complete content. If the file already exists from a previous run, overwrite it with the correct content and note the pre-existence in your report.

DOCUMENT REQUIREMENTS (exact):
1. First line/heading: title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" (use the document's Title or a Heading 0/1 style — make it clearly the document title).
2. Then a section (heading level 1) for EACH of the three papers, clearly identifying the paper. Suggested heading format: "1. Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv:2301.07041)" — each heading must contain the paper's exact title. Under each section include paragraphs describing:
   - the paper's title (explicitly, e.g. "Title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"),
   - its key contributions,
   - its methodology.
   (You may also include key findings and authors; the three required elements are title, key contributions, methodology.)
3. After the three individual sections, a final section titled exactly "Comparative Analysis" (heading level 1), drawing connections between the three papers and how they relate to each other in their contributions to large language model research. Base this ONLY on the canonical packet below. Suggested connective threads (use your judgment grounded in the packet): scaling laws (PAPER 1) provide the predictive framework for how capability grows with size/data/compute, which underpins the large-scale training choices and compute allocation relevant to the other two; InstructGPT (PAPER 2) builds on the GPT-3 line and adds a human-feedback alignment layer (SFT + reward model + PPO/RLHF), showing capability and alignment can be improved at much smaller scale; OPT (PAPER 3) is an open-source replication/extension of the GPT-3-style dense transformer line whose scale (125M–175B) and benchmark parity with GPT-3 make scaling-law and alignment research reproducible in the open. Together they span capability scaling, alignment via human feedback, and open reproducibility of large language model research.

CANONICAL THREE-PAPER PACKET (verbatim facts to use):

PAPER 1:
- arXiv ID: 2301.07041; Title: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"
- Authors (as returned by database): Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan
- Sections: Introduction; Scaling Laws; Experiments; Conclusion
- Key contributions: Empirical scaling laws for language model cross-entropy loss; loss follows a power law with model size (N), dataset size (D), and compute (C); principled framework for predicting performance and allocating a fixed compute budget optimally; architectural details (width/depth) have minimal effects within a wide range.
- Methodology: Trained over 1000 models spanning ~3 orders of magnitude in scale; systematically varied model size, dataset size, compute; fitted power laws L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N (analogous for D and C); analyzed overfitting vs model/dataset size and training speed vs model size.
- Key findings: Power-law exponents approx alpha_N = 0.076, alpha_D = 0.095, alpha_C = 0.050, trends spanning >7 orders of magnitude; larger models on more data/compute achieve lower loss; larger models more sample-efficient.

PAPER 2:
- arXiv ID: 2203.11171; Title: "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"
- Authors (as returned by database): Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang
- Sections: Introduction; Method; Experiments; Results
- Key contributions: Introduces InstructGPT; RLHF yields models strongly preferred by human labelers over much larger baselines; alignment gains (truthfulness, less toxicity) at small scale (1.3B vs 175B GPT-3).
- Methodology: Three steps starting from GPT-3: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstrations; (2) reward model trained from human preference comparisons; (3) PPO reinforcement learning fine-tuning with the reward model (RLHF).
- Key findings: InstructGPT 1.3B preferred to GPT-3 175B on 85% of prompts; more truthful on TruthfulQA; less toxic; alignment improvement with minimal trade-off in general capabilities.

PAPER 3:
- arXiv ID: 2205.01068; Title: "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models"
- Authors (as returned by database): Susan Zhang, Stephen Roller, Naman Goyal
- Sections: Introduction; Architecture; Training; Results
- Key contributions: Fully open-source LLM suite 125M–175B parameters; matches or exceeds GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks; releases weights and training code to enable community study of LLMs.
- Methodology: Standard transformer with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, learned positional embeddings; AdamW optimizer; ~800GB corpus (Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and others); tensor and pipeline parallelism on up to 992 A100 GPUs.
- Key findings: OPT-175B matches GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot benchmarks; full public release of weights and code; documents training methodology, hardware, and lessons from training at scale.

VERIFICATION (mandatory):
4. READ BACK the final document and validate: use mcp__word__get_document_text and mcp__word__get_document_outline (or read it back with python-docx) against the file at the target path. Confirm: (a) file exists at exact path; (b) document title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" present; (c) heading order is exactly: title, then the three paper sections (each heading contains the paper's exact title), then "Comparative Analysis"; (d) each paper section contains title/contributions/methodology text.
5. RETURN a structured report: absolute file path, file size, heading order as read back, exact paper-title coverage (each of the three exact titles present), presence of "Comparative Analysis", and validation result. Do NOT touch Notion or email.
